introduction: These hundred readings speak of capacity and readiness. Grace is like rain, they say, and falls on everything; what grows depends on the soil. A lamp whose oil and wick are ready lights at a touch, and a wet log does not. People are asked to enlarge their capacity daily, to thirst, to open eyes and ears, and at the same time they are told that faith is a gift and not a wage. Beside the readings stand the parables of sower, talents and lamps, the widow's borrowed vessels, the Qur’an's valleys that flow each according to its measure, and Confucius and Aristotle on learning. The harder sayings are there too: that it is not of him that willeth, that hearts and ears are given or withheld, that many are called and few chosen, with Mencius's farmer and Franklin's proverb on either side of the question.
questions: The readings say the bounty is universal and capacity varies. What in your own life has enlarged your capacity to receive something good?
One reading says that the intention itself is capacity. How far do you think wanting a thing prepares a person for it?
Paul says it is not of him that willeth; Franklin says God helps those who help themselves. How do you hold effort and grace together?
Deuteronomy and Isaiah speak of hearts and ears not given, or made heavy. What do you make of the idea that readiness itself may be withheld?
Jesus warns against casting pearls before swine, and the readings against judging who has capacity. How do you decide what to share, and with whom?
Mencius's farmer pulled at his corn to make it grow. Where are you tempted to force growth, in yourself or in someone else?

outside.why: Jesus said that the harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few.
Paul says that faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
Jesus said: ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.
James says bluntly: ye have not, because ye ask not; ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss.
Paul says: I have planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.
The Qur’an says that God tasketh not a soul beyond its scope.
Jesus said: blessed are they which do hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled.
Hosea says: break up your fallow ground, for it is time to seek the Lord.
The Letter to the Ephesians says: by grace are ye saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God.
Paul goes further: it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. If faith is a grace and not a wage, what is the point of striving for capacity?
Jesus said that the Father sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.
This is the verse the readings recall: the trust was offered to the heavens, the earth and the hills, and they shrank from bearing it, and man assumed it.
The Qur’an says that God sendeth down water from the sky, so that valleys flow according to their measure.
Elisha told a widow to borrow empty vessels, not a few, and the oil flowed until there was not a vessel more, and then it stayed.
In the parable one sowing falls by the way side, on stony places, among thorns and on good ground.
The Letter to the Ephesians says that unto every one is given grace according to the measure of the gift.
In the parable a man gave to one servant five talents, to another two, and to another one, to every man according to his several ability.
In the parable those hired at the eleventh hour receive the same as those who bore the burden and heat of the day. How does that story sit with stations reached by preparation?
Jesus said: whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance.
Aristotle taught that we learn by doing: men become builders by building, and just by doing just acts.
Paul says that there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit.
In the psalm God says: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.
Explaining his parable of the soils, Jesus said: the seed is the word of God.
In the parable five virgins had oil for their lamps when the bridegroom came, and five had none.
Shakespeare's Cassius says: the fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves. How much of a person's readiness is their own doing?
This is the verse the reading quotes: an oil that would almost glow forth of itself though no fire touched it.
Proverbs describes a neglected field, all grown over with thorns, its stone wall broken down.
The Qur’an says that the vegetation of the good land cometh forth by permission of its Lord, while from the bad only the useless cometh forth.
Isaiah says that as the rain cometh down and watereth the earth, so the word shall not return void.
Mencius tells of a man who, grieved that his corn was not taller, pulled at it to help it grow. Can capacity be hurried, in oneself or in others?

Moses tells Israel after forty years: the Lord hath not given you an heart to perceive, and eyes to see, unto this day. If the capacity to perceive is itself given or withheld, who is answerable for lacking it?
Jesus said: with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.
Isaiah calls: ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters.
The psalmist's soul pants after God as the hart pants after the water brooks.
Jesus told the woman at the well that whoever drinks of the water he gives shall never thirst.
Proverbs asks why there is a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he hath no heart to it.
Jesus said: neither cast ye your pearls before swine. How is that counsel to be kept without deciding too soon who lacks capacity?
Jesus said that he spoke in parables because seeing they see not, and hearing they hear not.
The Book of Revelation ends: whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
The psalmist says: my soul thirsteth for Thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is.
Seneca wrote that it is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor. What distinguishes the thirst that enlarges a soul from the craving that impoverishes it?
The council perceived that Peter and John were unlearned and ignorant men, and marvelled.
Paul reminds the Corinthians that not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble are called.
Jesus thanked the Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent and revealing them unto babes.
The elder brother in the parable had served many years and never transgressed, and stayed outside in anger. What can long religious practice do to a person's readiness?
Jesus ended a parable of a wedding feast with the words: many are called, but few are chosen.
Paul asks: what hast thou that thou didst not receive? If believing shows capacity, whose achievement is the capacity?
Paul writes that God hath mercy on whom He will, and asks who art thou that repliest against God. Is it a comfort or a difficulty to be told that one advanced because one was able?
Luke says of the boy Jesus that he increased in wisdom and stature.
Paul tells the Corinthians that he had to speak to them as unto babes.
The Letter to the Hebrews says that strong meat belongs to them that are of full age, whose senses are exercised by use.
Paul says: let us not be weary in well doing, for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Zechariah hears: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
A centurion said to Jesus: speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed.
Confucius said: I do not open up the truth to one who is not eager to get knowledge.
Jesus said: blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
Jesus said: walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you.
Jesus said that unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
Jesus told of a merchant who found one pearl of great price, and sold all that he had, and bought it.
Proverbs says: buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding.
The Letter to the Hebrews says of those once enlightened who fall away that it is impossible to renew them again. Is a lost opportunity ever beyond recovery?
The Qur’an says that it is not the eyes that grow blind, but the hearts within the bosoms.
Paul prays that the eyes of his friends' understanding may be enlightened.
In the Qur’an Jacob says, while the caravan is still far off: truly I am conscious of the breath of Joseph.
William Blake wrote that if the doors of perception were cleansed every thing would appear to man as it is, infinite.
Jesus told Nicodemus that except a man be born of water and of the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.
Jesus likened his generation to children saying: we have piped unto you, and ye have not danced.
Shakespeare's Lorenzo distrusts the man that hath no music in himself, nor is not moved with concord of sweet sounds.
Paul says that the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit, because they are spiritually discerned.
The man healed in John's Gospel says: whereas I was blind, now I see.
Wordsworth wrote of a man to whom a primrose by a river's brim was a yellow primrose, and it was nothing more. What does it take to see more in a thing than its name?
In the parable a Pharisee thanked God that he was not as other men, and a publican would not lift up his eyes, and the publican went home justified.
Paul says that we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the power may be of God, and not of us.
George Herbert asks: who would have thought my shrivelled heart could have recovered greenness?
James says that every good gift and every perfect gift is from above.
Augustine prayed in the Confessions: give what You command, and command what You will.
Benjamin Franklin's almanac has the proverb: God helps them that help themselves. Which comes first, the help or the effort?
Solomon, offered whatever he wished, asked for an understanding heart to discern between good and bad.
Jesus said that the wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou canst not tell whence it cometh.
Portia says that mercy droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven upon the place beneath.
The psalm invites: O taste and see that the Lord is good.
Jesus wept over the city, saying: if thou hadst known, in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace.
In the parable those invited to the supper sent their excuses: a piece of ground, five yoke of oxen, a wife.
Jesus told of a house on which the rain descended and the floods came and the winds blew, and it fell not, for it was founded upon a rock.
Jesus said that if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch.
John's Gospel says that men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.
John's Gospel says: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.
Isaiah is told: make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes. When a people is deprived, who has closed the ear?
Jesus said that new wine must be put into new bottles, and both are preserved.
The Light Verse ends: God guideth unto His light whom He will. How do you understand a bounty that is evident to all and reaches only some?
The first letter to Timothy says that God will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. If that is God's will, can anyone be finally without capacity?
Through Ezekiel God promises to take away the stony heart and give a heart of flesh. If a stone can be changed for flesh, is any heart beyond the rain?
The first letter of Peter says: as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.
Proverbs says: iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Paul says that now we see through a glass, darkly, and know in part.
Jesus told his disciples: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.
Isaiah says that God giveth power to the faint, and to them that have no might He increaseth strength.
The psalmist prays: open Thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of Thy law.
Elisha prayed, Lord, open his eyes that he may see, and the young man saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire.
Moses says that the word is not in heaven or beyond the sea, but very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth and in thy heart.

romans-not-of-him-that-willeth.text: So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy

kings-borrow-thee-vessels.text: Then he said, Go, borrow thee vessels abroad of all thy neighbours, even empty vessels; borrow not a few. And when thou art come in, thou shalt shut the door upon thee and upon thy sons, and shalt pour out into all those vessels, and thou shalt set aside that which is full. So she went from him, and shut the door upon her and upon her sons, who brought the vessels to her; and she poured out. And it came to pass, when the vessels were full, that she said unto her son, Bring me yet a vessel. And he said unto her, There is not a vessel more. And the oil stayed

proverbs-price-in-the-hand-of-a-fool.text: Wherefore is there a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing he hath no heart to it

deuteronomy-heart-to-perceive.text: Yet the Lord hath not given you an heart to perceive, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, unto this day

john-cannot-bear-them-now.text: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now

proverbs-instruction-to-a-wise-man.text: Reprove not a scorner, lest he hate thee: rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee. Give instruction to a wise man, and he will be yet wiser: teach a just man, and he will increase in learning

james-ye-have-not.text: ye have not, because ye ask not. Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts

ephesians-measure-of-the-gift.text: But unto every one of us is given grace according to the measure of the gift of Christ

luke-good-measure.text: Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom. For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again

quran-not-beyond-its-scope.text: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope

quran-good-land.text: As for the good land, its vegetation cometh forth by permission of its Lord; while as for that which is bad, only the useless cometh forth (from it). Thus do We recount the tokens for people who give thanks.

shakespeare-fault-not-in-our-stars.text: The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings
